sentences.text: He made the mistake of telling his brother.

Marek was fifteen and had recently become impossible in the specific way that fifteen-year-olds become impossible, which is that he had stopped being interested in anything and had started being interested in not being interested in things.
Tolek told him because he had to tell somebody.
He had been up the mountain three times by then and the knowledge had got too big to carry alone; it kept coming up in his throat at the dinner table.
Marek listened to the whole thing.
Then he said: "It's a bear." "I know it's a bear." "Bears sleep.
That's what they do.
It's the entire thing bears are known for." He was not being cruel.
That was somehow worse.
He was being reasonable, patiently, the way you are reasonable with somebody who is quite young.

"It'll wake up when it's hungry and go and eat something and you won't want to be sitting four metres away when it does." "The snow isn't melting round her." "The snow isn't melting because it's a north face and it's in shadow until half past two." Tolek had no answer to that, because it was true.
It was a north face and it was in shadow until half past two, and that fact had been sitting there the whole time being an excellent explanation for something that was not what was happening.
That is the trouble with a good reason.
It does not have to be the right one to be difficult to argue with.
Marek came up with him on the Saturday.
He came up in the way older brothers come, complaining about the walk and going too fast and stopping to wait with his hands on his hips.
At the edge of the snow he stopped complaining.

Tolek watched him look at the line — that clean straight edge running across the mountain like the top of a page — and then look down at the frost fences standing up in the grass, in April, at two in the afternoon, in the sun.
They went up to the hollow together and Marek looked at the bear for about ninety seconds and then turned round and went back down the mountain without saying anything at all.
He did not speak to Tolek for two days.

On the third day he came into the room where Tolek was doing his homework and stood in the doorway and said: "Don't tell Mum." "I wasn't going to." "Don't tell anybody." He was holding the door frame with one hand.
"You know what happens if you tell people.
Somebody rings the forestry office and they come up with a truck, and they'll be right to, because it's a bear and there's a school in the valley.
And they'll do it properly and humanely and everything and it will still be a truck coming up the mountain." Tolek had not thought that far.

He thought about it for a long time afterwards — that his brother, who was impossible, who had not been interested in anything for a year and a half, had gone up the mountain, looked at a sleeping animal for ninety seconds, and immediately understood the whole shape of the danger while Tolek was still working out how to describe the frost.
"Are you coming up again?" Marek asked.
"Yes." His brother nodded slowly, and looked at the floor, and said, "Take the red coat, not that one.
That one's too thin and Mum'll notice you shivering." And he went out and shut the door.
They never discussed it again.
Not that spring, not that summer, not in the thirteen years afterwards while their mother was alive, and not at the funeral, and not since.
But Marek asked him one thing, at the funeral, standing at the back with a paper cup of coffee, out of nowhere, after a silence of about four minutes.
"That thing on the mountain," he said.
"Did it ever wake up?" And Tolek said: "No.
Not while I was there." And Marek said, "Right," and they went back in.
